subcomponents.title: Uses scene-kit APIs without bypassing or duplicating them

criteria.rationale: Talk.tsx renders the kit's Presentation with steps, title and initialMode. The shared Scene.tsx draws every entity with kit primitives (Box, Label, SymbolChip, Arrow, Frame) inside SceneLayer, wrapped in Appear. It builds nothing custom for layout morphing, exit animation or step navigation. Each step supplies the kit's Step contract (Scene, groupKey, payload), and Stage handles mounting and transitions. The demo does not bypass or reimplement kit mechanisms.
evidence: Talk.tsx: `<Presentation steps={STEPS} title={TITLE} initialMode="browse" />` imported from presentation-kit/index.ts.
Scene.tsx: `render()` returns Box, Label, SymbolChip, Arrow and Frame, each given `layoutId={e.id}` and x/y/w/h. `Scene` wraps them in `<SceneLayer>` and `<Appear key={e.id} enter={e.from ==…
steps.ts: `STEPS` maps NARRATION to `Step<Payload>` objects with `Scene`, `groupKey: 'how-to'` and `payload: { stage: i + 1 }`.
presentation-kit/Presentation.tsx and Stage.tsx: the kit provides the nav hook, Stage, LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence. The demo has no motion or navigation code of its own.
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Uses stable identities and appropriate grouped-scene architecture

criteria.rationale: Grouping: steps.ts builds all nine steps from NARRATION.map with the same `Scene` and `groupKey: 'how-to'`. sceneKey() turns that into a single key `group:how-to:<sceneId>`. Stage uses that key on its motion.div, so the scene instance stays mounted across all nine steps and only `payload.stage` changes. A single shared groupKey is the correct grouping for this deck. Identity: entities.ts gives every entity a presentation-owned id via `ns(...)`. Scene.tsx passes `e.id` as `layoutId` to Box, Label, SymbolChip, Arrow and Frame, and the Appear key is also `e.id`. The kit nodes forward layoutId to motion layoutId (EntityNode; Arrow directly) and also emit it as data-presentation-entity. The same ids are rendered in consecutive steps because `entitiesAt(stage)` filters on `from <= stage`. Each entity has one fixed position, so the identity chain is in place even though nothing moves. FLAGGED_CARD is consumed in Scene.tsx's emphasis check. Every entity is rendered with a layoutId, so none is a dead constant.
evidence: steps.ts: `Scene, groupKey: 'how-to', payload: { stage: i + 1 }` is applied to all nine NARRATION items.
sceneKey.ts: `step.groupKey ? `group:${step.groupKey}:${sceneId(step.Scene)}` : `step:${step.id}``.
Stage.tsx: `<motion.div key={sceneKey(step)}>` renders `<step.Scene payload={step.payload} .../>` inside LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence.
entities.ts: `ns = name => `how-to:${name}``. ENTITIES is filtered by `entitiesAt`, and FLAGGED_CARD = ns('card-2').
Scene.tsx: `layoutId={e.id}` on every primitive, and `emphasis={e.id === FLAGGED_CARD && stage >= 8}` on the card Box.
EntityNode.tsx: `layout layoutId={layoutId} data-presentation-entity={layoutId}`. Box, Label, SymbolChip and Frame delegate to EntityNode. Arrow.tsx sets `layoutId={layoutId}` on motion.svg.
judging basis: consensus-pass

subcomponents.title: Maintains clear boundaries and scope discipline

criteria.rationale: The demo splits cleanly into four presentation-local modules. narration.ts holds plain data and TITLE. entities.ts holds the entity namespace and geometry. steps.ts maps narration to Step objects. Scene.tsx renders them, and Talk.tsx composes the result. The kit stays topic-agnostic. The required title input is passed from Talk.tsx (`title={TITLE}`) into Presentation. Presentation consumes it by writing it to the root element's `data-presentation-title-text` attribute. Its value is not shown visibly, but it is consumed rather than ignored. The visible titles come from each step's title. The registry's literal title string duplicates TITLE, which is minor. The entity constants (ENTITIES, entitiesAt, ns, FLAGGED_CARD) are all imported and used in Scene.tsx or steps.ts. The kit constants I checked are used in the kit: MIN_SCALE, SWIPE_MIN_PX, WIDE_VIEWPORT and ENTER_DELAY.

Presentation.tsx destructures `title` and emits `data-presentation-title-text={title}` on the root element.
Scene.tsx imports `FLAGGED_CARD` and `entitiesAt` from entities.ts and uses both.
presentations/index.ts holds a one-line registry entry that lazy-loads Talk.tsx.
narration.ts is plain data with no JSX.

criteria.rationale: startPreview reserves a fresh ephemeral port itself via freePort() and starts vite preview on it with --strictPort. Readiness is Promise.race([waitReady(...), exited]). criteria.rationale: The primitives type their props from the element props: NodeProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, ArrowProps extends SVGAttributes<SVGSVGElement>, EmphasisProps extends HTMLAttributes<HTMLSpanElement>, and SceneLayer uses React.HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>. No Record<string, unknown> bag is used. Identity hooks come after the caller spread: EntityNode puts layoutId, data-presentation-node and data-presentation-entity after {...rest}, Arrow puts layoutId and its data-presentation hooks after {...rest}, and Emphasis and SceneLayer do the same. Kit-only props (kind, Icon, emphasis, label, via, from, to, bidirectional, canvas, active, enter) are destructured out, so they do not reach the DOM.
evidence: src/presentation-kit/nodes/shared.ts NodeProps extends Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLElement>, ...>.
src/presentation-kit/nodes/EntityNode.tsx: `<motion.div {...(rest as object)} layout layoutId={layoutId} ... data-presentation-node={kind} data-presentation-entity={layoutId}>`.
src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx destructures from, to, via, bidirectional and canvas, then sets layoutId and data-presentation-* after the spread.
src/presentation-kit/nodes/Box.tsx and Frame.tsx destructure Icon, emphasis and label.
src/presentation-kit/nodes/Emphasis.tsx and SceneLayer.tsx put data-presentation attributes after {...rest}.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: The tests that exercise a browser do so only by running verify.mjs or inspect-presentation.mjs as child processes (e2e, INT-001, INT-002). None of those test files calls waitForTimeout, setTimeout or any sleep, and they assert only on process output, exit codes and artifacts. The scripts under test wait for the step index with waitForFunction on data-step-index.
evidence: tests/e2e/verify-pass.test.ts and tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts use run('npm'|'node', ...) and assert on the output.
tests/integration/int-002-inspect.test.ts uses run() in beforeAll and asserts on the captures.
A grep of tests/ for waitForTimeout, setTimeout and sleep matched no test file.
judging basis: consensus-pass

criteria.rationale: Every preview the tests start comes from startPreview, which picks its port with freePort() (listen on port 0), so no fixed port is shared. The stub-preview unit test calls p.stop() and asserts the pid is gone. The e2e and integration tests start verify/inspect as child processes, and the exit assertions run through alive(pid) for the preview pid printed by the script. The server itself is spawned directly from node, not through an npm/npx wrapper. The only hardcoded 4173 is in a pure urlFor() string test and starts no server.
evidence: scripts/lib/preview.mjs: `const chosen = port ?? (await freePort())`.
tests/unit/scripts.test.ts 'starts the preview ... stop() kills it': await p.stop(); expect(() => process.kill(p.pid, 0)).toThrow().

tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts expectFailure: if (pid) expect(alive(pid)).toBe(false).
tests/integration/int-002-inspect.test.ts: expect(alive(pid)).toBe(false).

responses.question_text: Across the full presentation, how good do the titles, captions, labels, and other content text look and read? Judge whether important content text is visibly present, typography, sizing, weight, spacing, line breaks, contrast, legibility, visual hierarchy, and whether the wording is clear, intentional, and audience-ready rather than sounding like an internal annotation. Do not judge navigation controls or presentation chrome here, and do not judge the placement or styling of non-text elements.

How well designed are the individual scene elements, such as boxes, arrows, icons, illustrations, and diagram nodes? Judge their shapes, proportions, fills, borders, detail, consistency, and overall craft. Do not judge their text, placement, movement, or navigation chrome here.

At a normal wide viewport, how well are the text and visual elements arranged relative to one another? Judge alignment, spacing, grouping, balance, focal points, use of space, and whether anything feels crowded, disconnected, clipped, or unintentionally overlapping. Judge viewport adaptation separately under responsive visual quality.

As you advance through the presentation, how well do the animations and scene changes work? Judge smoothness, pacing, meaningful entrances and exits, continuity of persistent elements, and whether each step visibly evolves the existing scene instead of feeling like an unrelated replacement.

Taken as a whole, how strong is the presentation’s visual identity? Judge its color palette, background treatment, stylistic consistency, brand character, polish, memorability, and whether it feels intentionally designed and finished. Judge the craft of individual scene elements separately.

How clear, discoverable, and visually integrated are the presentation controls and chrome? Judge progress indicators, previous/next controls, table of contents, mode switching, and attribution. Focus on their appearance and ease of understanding, not whether every input method technically works or how content captions are styled.

Compare the presentation at wide and narrow viewport sizes. How well does its hierarchy and composition adapt? Judge scaling, density, readability, control accessibility, clipping, overlap, and whether the narrow version still feels intentionally composed. Judge baseline wide-screen composition separately.

votes.rationale: Grouping: steps.ts builds all nine steps from NARRATION.map with the same `Scene` and `groupKey: 'how-to'`. sceneKey() turns that into a single key `group:how-to:<sceneId>`. Stage uses that key on its motion.div, so the scene instance stays mounted across all nine steps and only `payload.stage` changes. A single shared groupKey is the correct grouping for this deck. Identity: entities.ts gives every entity a presentation-owned id via `ns(...)`. Scene.tsx passes `e.id` as `layoutId` to Box, Label, SymbolChip, Arrow and Frame, and the Appear key is also `e.id`. The kit nodes forward layoutId to motion layoutId (EntityNode; Arrow directly) and also emit it as data-presentation-entity. The same ids are rendered in consecutive steps because `entitiesAt(stage)` filters on `from <= stage`. Each entity has one fixed position, so the identity chain is in place even though nothing moves. FLAGGED_CARD is consumed in Scene.tsx's emphasis check. Every entity is rendered with a layoutId, so none is a dead constant.

Presentation consumes it by writing it to the root element's `data-presentation-title-text` attribute. Its value is not shown visibly, but it is consumed rather than ignored. The visible titles come from each step's title. The registry's literal title string duplicates TITLE, which is minor. The entity constants (ENTITIES, entitiesAt, ns, FLAGGED_CARD) are all imported and used in Scene.tsx or steps.ts. The kit constants I checked are used in the kit: MIN_SCALE, SWIPE_MIN_PX, WIDE_VIEWPORT and ENTER_DELAY.

presentations/index.ts holds a one-line registry entry that lazy-loads Talk.tsx.

votes.rationale: startPreview reserves a fresh ephemeral port itself via freePort() and starts vite preview on it with --strictPort. Readiness is Promise.race([waitReady(...), exited]). 'exited' is an event-driven promise that rejects on the child's 'exit' event. It is not liveness sampled before each request. If the child exits at any point before readiness, for example because the port is busy, the race rejects. startPreview then stops the child and throws, and verify.mjs turns that into a render-phase failure. This is mechanism (b). A unit test with a stub vite that exits at startup asserts the rejection. The e2e tests assert the preview pid is dead after failure.

checks.rationale: The auditor's claim does not hold. The gap it describes is real in the code, but nothing the candidate actually runs can reach it. In both inspect copies, `inspectPresentation` calls `log(...)` once, after `startPreview` returns and before the `try` block. That call's only inputs are `urlFor(preview.port)`, a plain template string, and `preview.pid`. The default `log` is `console.log`. The CLI entry point never passes a different `log`. The inspect test runs the script through that CLI. So the auditor's scenario only happens if a caller passes in a `log` function that throws, which is a hypothetical input the candidate never produces. The contract says not to fail on such inputs. The guidance does name 'an error thrown after the preview started', but that covers errors the candidate can produce. Every such error happens inside the `try` and reaches the `finally` that awaits `preview.stop()`: a browser launch failure, a failed `goto`, a `waitFor` timeout, a step that does not advance, and capture errors. `preview.stop()` sends SIGTERM to the `node vite.js preview` child itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. It falls back to SIGKILL and waits for the child's 'exit' event. `startPreview` also stops the child if it is not ready in time. Both verify copies stop the preview in a `finally` that every path goes through. The rubric therefore does not treat the cited fact as defeating the pass verdict.

votes.rationale: startPreview reserves a fresh ephemeral port itself via freePort() and starts vite preview on it with --strictPort. Readiness is Promise.race([waitReady(...), exited]). 'exited' is an event-driven promise that rejects on the child's 'exit' event. It is not liveness sampled before each request. engineering-quality.rationale: The auditor's claim does not hold. The gap it describes is real in the code, but nothing the candidate actually runs can reach it. In both inspect copies, `inspectPresentation` calls `log(...)` once, after `startPreview` returns and before the `try` block. That call's only inputs are `urlFor(preview.port)`, a plain template string, and `preview.pid`. The default `log` is `console.log`. The CLI entry point never passes a different `log`. The inspect test runs the script through that CLI. So the auditor's scenario only happens if a caller passes in a `log` function that throws, which is a hypothetical input the candidate never produces. The contract says not to fail on such inputs. The guidance does name 'an error thrown after the preview started', but that covers errors the candidate can produce. Every such error happens inside the `try` and reaches the `finally` that awaits `preview.stop()`: a browser launch failure, a failed `goto`, a `waitFor` timeout, a step that does not advance, and capture errors. `preview.stop()` sends SIGTERM to the `node vite.js preview` child itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. It falls back to SIGKILL and waits for the child's 'exit' event. `startPreview` also stops the child if it is not ready in time. Both verify copies stop the preview in a `finally` that every path goes through. The rubric therefore does not treat the cited fact as defeating the pass verdict.

engineering-quality.rationale: This criterion is about the delivered automated tests that drive a browser. The fixed sleeps the auditor cites are in the product's verify and inspect tooling, not in the test files. The browser-facing tests are the E2E, integration and jsdom unit tests. None of them sleeps for a fixed time. The E2E and integration tests start the scripts through run(), which resolves only when the child process closes, so awaiting it does wait for the run to finish. They then check the exit code, the output and the files the scripts wrote. The jsdom tests use waitFor polling. INT-002 checks waitedMs >= 700 to test the inspect helper's documented --settle feature. That is an assertion about the product's behaviour, not a sleep inside the test. In renderSample, the step index is waited on with a waitForFunction poll, not the settleMs delay. The inspect settle interval is the helper's configurable feature, and its waitStable loop polls observable state. The guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as noise. The stated reason therefore does not defeat the pass.
